claim: D. melanogaster larvae are soft bodied cylindrical organisms about 4 mm in length and about 800 μm in diameter in the third instar stage.
source: The larva is a soft bodied cylindrical organism about 4 mm in length and about 800 μm in diameter in the third instar stage.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript providing anatomical measurements of the organism.

claim: D. melanogaster larvae move by exploiting the peristaltic propagation of muscular relaxation and contraction waves along their bodies to induce forward locomotion.
source: It moves in a manner similar to other long soft-bodied creatures such as earthworms and leeches by exploiting the peristaltic propagation of muscular relaxation and contraction waves along their bodies to induce forward locomotion, or crawling (Trueman, 1975)
evidence: Statement supported by citation to Trueman, 1975.

claim: Eliminating proprioception with genetic and optogenetic methods leads to peristaltic waves with a period that is approximately 4 times longer or may even stop propagating.
source: Eliminating proprioception with genetic (Hughes and Thomas, 2007) and optogenetic (Inada et al., 2011) methods leads to qualitative changes in the crawling gait: peristaltic waves have a period that is ≈4 times longer or may even stop propagating (Song et al., 2007)
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: Eliminating proprioception causes body segments to contract approximately 2 times more.
source: body segments contract ≈2 times more (Hughes and Thomas, 2007)
evidence: Statement supported by citation to Hughes and Thomas, 2007.

claim: Experiments that block sensory input in the embryo show that crawling behavior still develops in the larva, but with longer peristaltic wave periods.
source: Experiments that block sensory input in the embryo show that crawling behavior still develops in the larva, but with longer peristaltic wave periods (Suster and Bate, 2002; Fushiki et al., 2013)
evidence: Statement supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The mathematical model couples excitation-inhibition circuits in the nervous system to force production in the muscles and body movement in a frictional environment.
source: Our model couples the excitation-inhibition circuits in the nervous system to force production in the muscles and body movement in a frictional environment, thence linking neural dynamics to body mechanics via sensory feedback in a heterogeneous environment.
evidence: Direct statement in the abstract describing the model structure.

claim: The model explains the basic observed phenomenology of crawling with and without proprioception.
source: Our results explain the basic observed phenomenology of crawling with and without proprioception, and elucidate the stabilizing role that proprioception plays in producing a robust crawling phenotype in the presence of biological perturbations.
evidence: Statement in the abstract describing model results.

claim: Proprioception plays a stabilizing role in producing a robust crawling phenotype in the presence of biological perturbations.
source: Our results explain the basic observed phenomenology of crawling with and without proprioception, and elucidate the stabilizing role that proprioception plays in producing a robust crawling phenotype in the presence of biological perturbations.
evidence: Statement in the abstract describing model findings about proprioception.

claim: The larva has 3 thoracic (T1-T3) and 8 abdominal (A1-A8) segments.
source: Anatomically, the larva has 3 thoracic (T1-T3) and 8 abdominal (A1-A8) segments, Figure 1A.
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 1A showing anatomical structure.

claim: The head is treated as part of the T1 segment and the tail as part of the A8 segment in the model.
source: We therefore treat the head as a part of the T1 segment, and the tail as a part of the A8 segment.
evidence: Direct statement describing modeling assumptions.

claim: Larvae lift segments off the ground when they contract.
source: Larvae lift segments off the ground when they contract (Heckscher et al., 2012)
evidence: Statement supported by citation to Heckscher et al., 2012.

claim: The model uses Wilson-Cowan equations for the activity of excitatory and inhibitory populations of neurons in a segment.
source: We model the neural dynamics of the ventral nerve chord (VNC) in terms of the classical Wilson-Cowan equations (Wilson and Cowan, 1972) for the activity of excitatory and inhibitory populations of neurons in a segment.
evidence: Direct statement describing the mathematical model with citation.

claim: Larvae can crawl without proprioceptive feedback.
source: Observations show that larvae can crawl without proprioceptive feedback (Suster and Bate, 2002; Hughes and Thomas, 2007; Inada et al., 2011)
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: Larvae can crawl without input from the brain.
source: Observations show that larvae can crawl without proprioceptive feedback (Suster and Bate, 2002; Hughes and Thomas, 2007; Inada et al., 2011) or input from the brain (Berni et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to Berni et al., 2012.

claim: The central nervous system, when isolated from the body, can still produce waves of neural activity propagating from posterior to anterior.
source: Furthermore, the central nervous system, when isolated from the body, can still produce waves of neural activity propagating from posterior to anterior (Pulver et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to Pulver et al., 2015.

claim: Inertial effects are negligible in larval segment movement.
source: Further, since the maggot and its segments move relatively slowly, we assume that inertial effects are negligible so that segmental forces are balanced by friction locally.
evidence: Statement describing a modeling assumption with justification provided.

claim: The mass of a third instar larva is approximately 10^-3 g.
source: The mass of a third instar larva is ≈10-3 g and the acceleration of the larvae is on the order of ≈10-3 m/s2, which leads to an inertial force of ≈10-6 gm/s2.
evidence: Direct statement providing quantitative estimate.

claim: The model predicts a speed of approximately 0.5 mm/s for third instar larvae.
source: Combining the time scale estimate and the length of the third instar larvae, our model predicts a speed of ≈0.5 mm/s, comparable with the observed speed of ≈1 mm/s (estimated from Figure 1 of Hughes and Thomas, [2007]).
evidence: Statement describing model prediction and comparison with experimental data.

claim: The observed speed of third instar larvae is approximately 1 mm/s.
source: Combining the time scale estimate and the length of the third instar larvae, our model predicts a speed of ≈0.5 mm/s, comparable with the observed speed of ≈1 mm/s (estimated from Figure 1 of Hughes and Thomas, [2007]).
evidence: Statement citing experimental observation from Hughes and Thomas, 2007.

claim: First instar larvae produce 0.5-1.5 waves per second.
source: Heckscher et. al. Heckscher et al. (2012) give a range of 0.5 − 1.5 waves produced per second
evidence: Statement citing experimental findings from Heckscher et al., 2012.

claim: The model predicts a speed range of approximately 30-90 μm/s for first instar larvae.
source: Combining the time scale estimate and the length of the first instar larvae, our model predicts a speed range of ≈30 − 90 μm/s, in agreement with the range reported in (Heckscher et al., 2012): ≈40 − 125 μm/s.
evidence: Statement describing model prediction and comparison with experimental data.

claim: The observed speed range for first instar larvae is approximately 40-125 μm/s.
source: Combining the time scale estimate and the length of the first instar larvae, our model predicts a speed range of ≈30 − 90 μm/s, in agreement with the range reported in (Heckscher et al., 2012): ≈40 − 125 μm/s.
evidence: Statement citing experimental observation from Heckscher et al., 2012.

claim: Peak segmental contraction, averaged over segments and waves, is approximately 30%.
source: Furthermore, we find that peak segmental contraction, averaged over segments and waves, is ≈30%, consistent with observations (Hughes and Thomas, 2007).
evidence: Statement describing simulation results and comparison with experimental observations.

claim: When segment-to-segment propagation was perturbed with optogenetic inhibition of motor neurons in a VNC segment, crawling stopped when the wave reached that segment.
source: When segment-to-segment propagation was perturbed with optogenetic inhibition of motor neurons in a VNC segment (Inada et al., 2011), crawling stopped when the wave reached that segment.
evidence: Statement citing experimental findings from Inada et al., 2011.

claim: When optogenetic inhibition is removed after up to 10 s, the larva resumed crawling from the same segment.
source: Conversely, when the inhibition is removed after up to 10 s, the larva resumed crawling from the same segment.
evidence: Statement citing experimental findings from Inada et al., 2011.

claim: Period-positive median segmental interneurons (PMSIs) are activated slightly later than the motor neurons in the same segment during forward crawling.
source: Specifically, during forward crawling, period-positive median segmental interneurons (PMSIs) were found to be activated slightly later than the motor neurons in the same segment (Kohsaka et al., 2014)
evidence: Statement citing experimental findings from Kohsaka et al., 2014.

claim: Optogenetic activation of PMSIs leads to inhibition of motor neuron activity locally, arresting peristaltic crawling.
source: their optogenetic activation leads to inhibition of motor neuron activity locally, arresting peristaltic crawling.
evidence: Statement citing experimental findings from Kohsaka et al., 2014.

claim: Silencing proprioceptive feedback using genetic and optogenetic methods leads to an increase in peak segmental contraction from approximately 30% to approximately 65%.
source: In another set of experiments, it was shown that silencing proprioceptive feedback to VNC using genetic (Hughes and Thomas, 2007; Suster and Bate, 2002) and optogenetic (Inada et al., 2011) methods leads to an increase in peak segmental contraction from ≈30% to ≈65% (Hughes and Thomas, 2007)
evidence: Statement citing experimental findings from multiple studies.

claim: Silencing proprioceptive feedback leads to a reduction in crawling rate to approximately one fourth.
source: and a reduction in rate to approximately one fourth (Inada et al., 2011)
evidence: Statement citing experimental findings from Inada et al., 2011.

claim: Silencing proprioceptive feedback leads to a reduction in crawling rate to approximately one tenth.
source: and to one tenth (Hughes and Thomas, 2007)
evidence: Statement citing experimental findings from Hughes and Thomas, 2007.

claim: With purely neural coupling (no proprioception), the model produces sustained crawling with only a single segment off-the-ground at a time.
source: With purely neural coupling, the model still produces sustained crawling but with a qualitative change in the crawling pattern (Figure 4 and Video 5). Only a single segment is off-the-ground at a time
evidence: Statement describing simulation results with reference to Figure 4 and Video 5.

claim: With purely neural coupling, peak segmental contraction increases to approximately 65% of segmental length.
source: while peak segmental contraction, averaged over all segments, increases to ≈65% of segmental length (≈70% for only A3-A4 segmental distance, Figure 4E)
evidence: Statement describing simulation results with reference to Figure 4E.

claim: With purely neural coupling, the larva produces a reduced rate of approximately 0.01 waves per τE.
source: the larva produces a reduced rate of ≈0.01 waves per τE and moves with speed ≈0.01⁢L/τE (Figure 4A and D), in agreement with experiments.
evidence: Statement describing simulation results with reference to Figure 4A and D, and comparison with experiments.

claim: A spatially coordinated CPG is not necessary for crawling.
source: This shows that a spatially coordinated CPG is not necessary for crawling, as was also suggested and shown in the simpler model put forward in (Paoletti and Mahadevan, 2014).
evidence: Statement describing model findings with citation to previous work.

claim: Proprioception increases robustness of locomotory behavior by providing a wider range of neural coupling over which sustained crawling can be achieved.
source: This manipulation suggests that proprioception increases robustness of locomotory behavior in two distinct ways. First, there is a wider range of neural coupling over which sustained crawling can be achieved.
evidence: Statement describing model findings based on parameter manipulations.

claim: Decreasing friction below slippage threshold should lead to higher speed with larger step sizes but a smaller number of waves per unit time.
source: In particular, decreasing friction below slippage threshold should lead to a higher speed with larger step sizes but a smaller number of waves per unit time, another testable prediction.
evidence: Statement describing model predictions.

claim: There should be much more variability in crawling metrics among individuals with silenced or weakened proprioception.
source: Interpreting this variation in parameters to that due to variations across individuals in a population, we predict that there should be much more variability in crawling metrics among individuals with silenced or weakened proprioception, a scenario amenable to testing using existing genetic tools (Hughes and Thomas, 2007; Inada et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement describing model predictions with citations to relevant experimental tools.

claim: Neural coupling may be used to control speed, with increased neural coupling leading to higher speeds.
source: Neural coupling may be used to control speed. Indeed, our model predicts that increase in neural coupling leads to higher speeds, even in the presence of proprioception.
evidence: Statement describing model predictions.

claim: In stick insects, slow, steady-walking is mainly coordinated by local proprioceptive signals but faster motion is driven by increased neural coupling between legs.
source: This suggestion is supported by experiments in stick insects, which show that slow, steady-walking is mainly coordinated by local proprioceptive signals but faster motion is driven by increased neural coupling between legs (Büschges, 2012).
evidence: Statement citing experimental findings from Büschges, 2012.

claim: The model reproduces the robust crawling gait consistent with experimental findings in first and third instar larvae.
source: This allows us to reproduce the robust crawling gait that is consistent with experimental findings in first (Heckscher et al., 2012) and third (Hughes and Thomas, 2007) instar larvae.
evidence: Statement describing model results with citations to experimental studies.

claim: The model qualitatively and quantitatively captures the effects of optogenetic perturbations of neural activity.
source: Furthermore, our model qualitatively and quantitatively captures the effects of a) optogenetic perturbations of neural activity (Inada et al., 2011; Kohsaka et al., 2014)
evidence: Statement describing model results with citations to experimental studies.

claim: The model qualitatively and quantitatively captures the effects of silencing proprioception with genetic and optogenetic methods.
source: and b) silencing proprioception with genetic (Hughes and Thomas, 2007) and optogenetic (Inada et al., 2011) methods.
evidence: Statement describing model results with citations to experimental studies.

claim: The head and tail of a larva move concurrently in a motion called the 'visceral piston phase' of crawling at the beginning of each crawling cycle.
source: At the beginning of each crawling cycle, it has been observed that the head and the tail of a larva move concurrently in a motion called the 'visceral piston phase' of crawling (Heckscher et al., 2012; Simon et al., 2010)
evidence: Statement citing experimental observations from Heckscher et al., 2012 and Simon et al., 2010.

claim: The gut moves with the head and the tail in advance of the surrounding body tissues during the visceral piston phase.
source: because the gut moves with the head and the tail, in advance of the surrounding body tissues.
evidence: Statement describing experimental observations.

claim: The model implements head-tail coupling by forcing the displacement of head and tail segments to be the same.
source: We model this behavior by forcing the displacement of head and tail segments to be the same.
evidence: Statement describing modeling approach.

claim: The peristaltic wave propagates to the tail through assumed long range neural and proprioceptive couplings of T2 and A8 segments once it reaches the head.
source: Once the peristaltic wave reaches the head, it propagates to the tail through assumed long range neural and proprioceptive couplings of T2 and A8 segments, and a new wave is initiated.
evidence: Statement describing model mechanism.

claim: The model shows that head and tail segments move together in the visceral piston phase followed by a peristaltic wave propagating from posterior to anterior segments.
source: We see that head and tail segments move together in the visceral piston phase (Heckscher et al., 2012; Simon et al., 2010), followed by a peristaltic wave with neural activity leading in phase, followed by muscular and contraction activity (Figure 2), propagating from posterior to anterior segments.
evidence: Statement describing simulation results with reference to Figure 2 and citations to experimental studies.

claim: In the model, neural activity leads in phase, followed by muscular and contraction activity during the peristaltic wave.
source: followed by a peristaltic wave with neural activity leading in phase, followed by muscular and contraction activity (Figure 2)
evidence: Statement describing simulation results with reference to Figure 2.

claim: Crawling can be stopped by shutting down the activity of excitatory neurons in the most posterior segment by an inhibitory input.
source: Crawling can be stopped by shutting down the activity of excitatory neurons in the most posterior segment by an inhibitory input (see also section 3.1.2).
evidence: Statement describing simulation results.

claim: In the model, during a stop, the memory of crawling phase is kept in the contraction of the body and the proprioceptive channel.
source: In our model (Figure 3), during a stop, the memory of crawling phase is kept in the contraction of the body and the proprioceptive channel which drives the proprioceptive activity.
evidence: Statement describing model mechanism with reference to Figure 3.

claim: In Inada et al.'s experiments, it is possible to resume crawling even after the neighboring posterior segment to the one being inhibited completes a contraction and relaxes back to its equilibrium length.
source: In Inada et. al.'s experiments (Inada et al., 2011), it is possible to resume crawling even after the neighboring posterior segment to the one being inhibited completes a contraction and relaxes back to its equilibrium length (Figure 7 of (Inada et al., 2011)).
evidence: Statement citing experimental findings from Inada et al., 2011.

claim: Inada et al. propose that the memory of crawling phase is held in the VNC.
source: Hence, Inada et. al. propose that the memory is held in the VNC.
evidence: Statement citing proposal from Inada et al.

claim: In Inada et al.'s experiments, the memory of crawling phase can last as long as 10 s.
source: We also want to point that in (Inada et al., 2011) the memory can last as long as 10 s.
evidence: Statement citing experimental findings from Inada et al., 2011.

claim: When PMSIs are inhibited using genetic and optogenetic methods, speed of peristalsis greatly decreased.
source: Other observations on PMSIs (Kohsaka et al., 2014) that remain to be incorporated into future models are: when inhibited using genetic and optogenetic methods, speed of peristalsis greatly decreased
evidence: Statement citing experimental findings from Kohsaka et al., 2014.

claim: When PMSIs are inhibited, duration of motor neuron bursting and muscle contraction increased.
source: duration of motor neuron bursting and muscle contraction increased
evidence: Statement citing experimental findings from Kohsaka et al., 2014.

claim: When PMSIs are inhibited, degree of segmental contraction did not change.
source: however degree of segmental contraction did not change.
evidence: Statement citing experimental findings from Kohsaka et al., 2014.

claim: Glutamatergic Ventro-Lateral Interneurons (GVLIs) ceased locomotion in the same segment when optogenetically activated.
source: In a very recent experiment (Itakura et al., 2015), a new class of pre-motor inhibitory neurons, Glutamatergic Ventro-Lateral Interneurons (GVLIs), were identified (glutamate inhibits larva motor neurons (Rohrbough and Broadie, 2002)), which ceased locomotion in the same segment when optogenetically activated.
evidence: Statement citing experimental findings from Itakura et al., 2015.

claim: During unperturbed peristaltic wave propagation, GVLIs' activation lagged motor neurons by several segments.
source: During unperturbed peristaltic wave propagation, GVLIs' activation lagged motor neurons by several segments
evidence: Statement citing experimental findings from Itakura et al., 2015.

claim: GVLIs provide a contraction termination signal when the wave reaches anterior segments.
source: suggesting that GVLIs provide a contraction termination signal when the wave reaches anterior segments.
evidence: Statement citing interpretation from Itakura et al., 2015.

claim: Glutamate inhibits larva motor neurons.
source: (glutamate inhibits larva motor neurons (Rohrbough and Broadie, 2002))
evidence: Statement citing experimental findings from Rohrbough and Broadie, 2002.

claim: Neurons that extend across multiple segments have been observed in Drosophila larva VNC.
source: Such long range coupling, also used in stick insect models (Daun-Gruhn and Tóth, 2011), is plausible as neurons that extend across multiple segments have been observed in Drosophila larva VNC (Schmid et al., 1999).
evidence: Statement citing experimental observations from Schmid et al., 1999.

claim: The activity of the muscles that coordinate segment lifting are synchronized with the activity of muscles that provide contractile forces in the segment.
source: Indeed, activity of the muscles that coordinate segment lifting are synchronized with the activity of muscles that provide contractile forces in the segment (Heckscher et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement citing experimental findings from Heckscher et al., 2012.

claim: Segment-to-segment propagation of neural activity arises through posterior-to-anterior neural coupling between excitatory populations in adjacent segments and via proprioceptive coupling.
source: Our model shows that normal segment-to-segment propagation of activity arises through two different but coordinated channels, the posterior-to-anterior neural coupling between excitatory populations in adjacent segments, and via proprioceptive coupling (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: Statement describing model findings with reference to Figure 1C and D.

claim: Crawling metrics are robust until friction falls below a threshold (Fmax/kL∼0.4), when muscular forces become stronger than friction, leading to slippage.
source: Our main observation is that metrics of crawling are robust until friction falls below a threshold (Fm⁢a⁢x/k⁢L∼0.4), when muscular forces become stronger than friction, leading to slippage.
evidence: Statement describing simulation results.

claim: Below the friction threshold, the number of peristaltic waves per unit time drops.
source: Below the threshold, number of peristaltic waves per unit time drops (Figure 6B)
evidence: Statement describing simulation results with reference to Figure 6B.

claim: Below the friction threshold, segment-to-segment propagation delay in the VNC increases.
source: as is confirmed by increased segment-to-segment propagation delay in the VNC (Figure 6G).
evidence: Statement describing simulation results with reference to Figure 6G.

claim: With decreasing friction, speed first increases due to larger step sizes, even though the frequency of peristaltic waves decreases, but eventually saturates.
source: The speed of the larva (Figure 6C) also follows an interesting trend; with decreasing friction, speed first increases due to larger step sizes (Figure 6D), even though the frequency of peristaltic waves decreases (Figure 6B), but eventually saturates.
evidence: Statement describing simulation results with references to Figure 6B, C, and D.

claim: Peak contraction of segments increases with decreased friction.
source: Peak contraction of segments increase (Figure 6E) with decreased friction.
evidence: Statement describing simulation results with reference to Figure 6E.

claim: The model produces a robust, sustained crawling gait with metrics consistent with experimental findings.
source: Our theoretical model for the forward crawling of a D. melanogaster larva incorporates the coupled mechanics of the soft body, the neural dynamics of VNC and frictional interactions with the substrate, complementing earlier isolated studies of these sub-systems. It produces a robust, sustained crawling gait with metrics consistent with experimental findings (Heckscher et al., 2012; Hughes and Thomas, 2007)
evidence: Statement describing model results with citations to experimental studies.

claim: The model can reproduce qualitative and quantitative changes in crawling gait due to perturbations in proprioceptive and neural channels of segment-to-segment wave propagation.
source: and furthermore, can reproduce qualitative and quantitative changes in crawling gait due to perturbations in proprioceptive (Hughes and Thomas, 2007; Inada et al., 2011) and neural (Inada et al., 2011; Kohsaka et al., 2014) channels of segment-to-segment wave propagation.
evidence: Statement describing model results with citations to experimental studies.

claim: The demonstration of purely proprioceptive crawling challenges the central role of CPG in crawling locomotion.
source: While both in our model and in experiments (Hughes and Thomas, 2007; Heckscher et al., 2012), the larvae can crawl without any proprioception, albeit much slower, the demonstration of purely proprioceptive crawling challenges the central role of CPG in crawling locomotion.
evidence: Statement describing model findings and their implications with citations to experimental studies.
